Accuracy is 67.6%, so the pipeline runs but the construction is off. I'll check the attention pattern and how well the MLP features fit the target waves.

Attention patterns match the fitted form well (corr 0.997). The bottleneck is the MLP readout: a linear fit of cos/sin(w(a+b)) from the neuron features only reaches R² ≈ 0.55. I'll test whether the bias or the attention product terms cause this.

Without the attention product terms the fit reaches R² ≈ 0.95, so those products are the problem. Since ReLU is positively homogeneous, scaling the neuron input amplitude up shrinks the products' relative weight without changing the mechanism. I'll test the amplitude.

Scaling `W_in` scales the products too, since they arrive through the residual stream, so amplitude doesn't help. The real fix is structural. In the explanation, each head's value carries the frequency its pattern uses (head 0 with pattern 47 moves 47-frequency values). Then the attention products are same-frequency products that directly produce cos/sin(w(a+b)). I'll restructure so each head's values carry only specific frequencies and check the fit.
Accuracy dropped to 62%, so I'll check the per-frequency fit again to see which channels are failing.

The fit is still poor. Cross-frequency products (e.g. 47⊗37) from heads whose values carry other frequencies are large and corrupt the neuron features. I'll test a few head-to-frequency assignments and measure both readout R² and accuracy.

Option v gives accuracy 1.0 with readout R² ≈ 0.93. Heads 0 and 1 carry the explanation's 47 and 51 patterns, with same-frequency values. Heads 2 and 3 use uniform attention, which avoids cross-frequency product noise. I'll rewrite the build script cleanly with this final design and the "=" suppression applied to every head.
Self-test passes with 100% accuracy. I'll confirm the build runs within the 60-second limit.

said: I've read the task and the explanation. The plan is to build the embedding, attention, and MLP weights directly from the explanation, then fit only the MLP-to-readout map with closed-form least squares. I'll write the script in one go and then run it.
The self-test runs but accuracy is only 0.679. I'll check which readout frequencies the fit gets wrong.
The fit is poor even for frequency 3, which has 128 neurons. Bias-free ReLU neurons don't span cos(w(a+b)) well. I'll sweep the neuron bias to see whether it helps.
The bias sweep only tried positive biases, and per-frequency neuron subsets fit worse than the full set. I'll try negative biases too.
Bias 0 is the best of the negative values I tried. I'll check positive biases over the full fit before deciding how to proceed.

Bias 0 remains the best, so the ReLU design is the limit, not the bias. Before accepting that, I'll check that the neuron pre-activations match the intended cos(wa+φ)+cos(wb+φ) formula, to rule out a construction bug.

Neuron pre-activations match the intended formula (correlation ≈ 1), so the MLP is built correctly. But attention to '=' reaches 0.093, far above the ~1e-4 I expected from the −10 key. I'll check the raw scores to find out why.

The cause is the 1/√32 scaling in the attention scores, which my constants ignored. The effective score scale is 0.707 instead of 4, and the '=' penalty is −1.77 instead of −10. I'll scale both constants by √32 and rebuild.

Accuracy fell to 0.40. The earlier 0.68 came from the weak attention products, so the MLP needs the attention-difference terms (z0−z1), which the explanation describes. I'll re-read the script and add a scalar coupling κ that lets each neuron also read the difference features with the same phase pattern. Then I'll sweep κ.
Positive κ makes things worse. The sign of the product term may be the issue, so I'll try negative values.

Coupling κ doesn't help, so I'll set it to 0. Next I'll sweep the attention slope, since it changes how much the attention-weighted terms contribute, and keep whichever setting scores best on the self-test.
Smaller slopes score higher. I'll check the low end of that range before settling on a value.
Accuracy is still below the 0.679 from the first version, which had a weaker '=' penalty. I'll sweep that penalty as the last parameter.

A penalty of 1 gives the highest self-test accuracy (0.78), but it leaves about 9% attention on '=', while the explanation says about 0.2%. I'll keep the faithful setting (penalty 10, slope 0.707, κ=0), which gives 0.56, and report the trade-off. I'll also hard-code those defaults and remove the env-var hooks.

`build_weights.py` builds `weights.npz`, and `selftest.py` passes, but accuracy is only **56.2%** (mean correct-answer probability 0.548). That is well short of the original model, which is near-perfect. **What's in the construction** (all weights are set directly from `EXPLANATION.md`, except one closed-form fit): - **Embedding:** cos/sin of w_k·t for k ∈ {2, 3, 23, 37, 39}, plus a flag dimension for '=' and a constant dimension. - **Attention:** heads 0–1 (k=23) and 2–3 (k=39) use the fitted α/β scores, so attention to a and b is about 0.5 ± the stated linear term.
1.why: Low accuracy and high HS: its script uses the target's frequencies {2, 3, 23, 37, 39}, and the measured states align (HS 0.92), but the answers are wrong (accuracy 0.5624). The wrong detail is a layout bug, not the explanation: its constants line `SEP, BIAS, P0, P1, P2, P3, RO = 10, 11, 12, 22, 42, 52, 52` gives head 3's output (P3) and the readout (RO) the same residual dimensions 52–61, although its own docstring puts heads 2/3 at 42–51, so head 3's attention output is added onto the answer the unembedding reads. Re-running its own script with that one fix gives accuracy 1.0000 at HS 0.91 (other changes tested: head 3 moved to unused dimensions (P3 = 62), nothing else changed: accuracy 1.0000; neurons split in the explanation's proportions, scaled to all 512 (k=2: 0 neurons): accuracy 0.5719; its own accuracy-best '=' penalty (1 instead of 10): accuracy 0.7846). The slip is Haiku's own: nothing the agent was given suggests a layout (the starter script defines only the array shapes, and TASK.md and ARCHITECTURE.md name no dimensions). Its own docstring puts heads 2 and 3 together at dimensions 42–51 and the readout at 52–61, so the constants line should read P3 = 42; it reads 52, the readout's first dimension. It stopped by its own choice after 22 tool calls and 6.4 minutes, well within the 60-minute, $2 per-run budget (no turn cap was set: Claude Code's --max-turns was not used). Its 2 replicates were identical in everything checked — the same files given to the agent (identical SHA-256 hashes), prompt, model (claude-haiku-5-5), Claude Code 2.1.330, effort and grading — so nothing the agent could see differed except the unseedable sampling (outside its view, the runs ran at different times and the server-side model behind the name cannot be verified); they reached accuracy 0.9994 and 0.9986. So the bug occurred in 1 of 3 identical runs: a chance slip that the setup does not force, whose frequency so few runs barely constrain (95 % Clopper–Pearson interval 1%–91%). The agent never found the bug: it blamed the neurons (“Bias-free ReLU neurons don't span cos(w(a+b)) well.”), tuned constants around the bug (self-test peak 0.7846) and then kept the setting it judged more faithful to the explanation (“I'll keep the faithful setting (penalty 10, slope 0.707, κ=0), which gives 0.56, and report the trade-off.”).
1.why_short: Right frequencies, wrong answers: a layout bug in Haiku's own script: head 3 wrote into the answer dimensions (P3 = RO = 52); fixing it gives accuracy 1.0000. The agent blamed the neurons and never found it (bug in 1 of 3 identical runs)

said: I've read the task and the explanation. The plan is to build the embedding, attention, and MLP weights directly from the explanation, then fit only the MLP-to-readout map with closed-form least squares. I'll write the script in one go and then run it.
The self-test runs but accuracy is only 0.679. I'll check which readout frequencies the fit gets wrong.
The fit is poor even for frequency 3, which has 128 neurons. Bias-free ReLU neurons don't span cos(w(a+b)) well. I'll sweep the neuron bias to see whether it helps.
The bias sweep only tried positive biases, and per-frequency neuron subsets fit worse than the full set. I'll try negative biases too.
Bias 0 is the best of the negative values I tried. I'll check positive biases over the full fit before deciding how to proceed.

Bias 0 remains the best, so the ReLU design is the limit, not the bias. Before accepting that, I'll check that the neuron pre-activations match the intended cos(wa+φ)+cos(wb+φ) formula, to rule out a construction bug.

Neuron pre-activations match the intended formula (correlation ≈ 1), so the MLP is built correctly. But attention to '=' reaches 0.093, far above the ~1e-4 I expected from the −10 key. I'll check the raw scores to find out why.

The cause is the 1/√32 scaling in the attention scores, which my constants ignored. The effective score scale is 0.707 instead of 4, and the '=' penalty is −1.77 instead of −10. I'll scale both constants by √32 and rebuild.

Accuracy fell to 0.40. The earlier 0.68 came from the weak attention products, so the MLP needs the attention-difference terms (z0−z1), which the explanation describes. I'll re-read the script and add a scalar coupling κ that lets each neuron also read the difference features with the same phase pattern. Then I'll sweep κ.
Positive κ makes things worse. The sign of the product term may be the issue, so I'll try negative values.

Coupling κ doesn't help, so I'll set it to 0. Next I'll sweep the attention slope, since it changes how much the attention-weighted terms contribute, and keep whichever setting scores best on the self-test.
Smaller slopes score higher. I'll check the low end of that range before settling on a value.
Accuracy is still below the 0.679 from the first version, which had a weaker '=' penalty. I'll sweep that penalty as the last parameter.

A penalty of 1 gives the highest self-test accuracy (0.78), but it leaves about 9% attention on '=', while the explanation says about 0.2%. I'll keep the faithful setting (penalty 10, slope 0.707, κ=0), which gives 0.56, and report the trade-off. I'll also hard-code those defaults and remove the env-var hooks.

`build_weights.py` builds `weights.npz`, and `selftest.py` passes, but accuracy is only **56.2%** (mean correct-answer probability 0.548). That is well short of the original model, which is near-perfect. **What's in the construction** (all weights are set directly from `EXPLANATION.md`, except one closed-form fit): - **Embedding:** cos/sin of w_k·t for k ∈ {2, 3, 23, 37, 39}, plus a flag dimension for '=' and a constant dimension. - **Attention:** heads 0–1 (k=23) and 2–3 (k=39) use the fitted α/β scores, so attention to a and b is about 0.5 ± the stated linear term.
2.why: Low accuracy and high HS: its script uses the target's frequencies {2, 3, 23, 37, 39}, and the measured states align (HS 0.92), but the answers are wrong (accuracy 0.5624). The wrong detail is a layout bug, not the explanation: its constants line `SEP, BIAS, P0, P1, P2, P3, RO = 10, 11, 12, 22, 42, 52, 52` gives head 3's output (P3) and the readout (RO) the same residual dimensions 52–61, although its own docstring puts heads 2/3 at 42–51, so head 3's attention output is added onto the answer the unembedding reads. Re-running its own script with that one fix gives accuracy 1.0000 at HS 0.91 (other changes tested: head 3 moved to unused dimensions (P3 = 62), nothing else changed: accuracy 1.0000; neurons split in the explanation's proportions, scaled to all 512 (k=2: 0 neurons): accuracy 0.5719; its own accuracy-best '=' penalty (1 instead of 10): accuracy 0.7846). The slip is Haiku's own: nothing the agent was given suggests a layout (the starter script defines only the array shapes, and TASK.md and ARCHITECTURE.md name no dimensions). Its own docstring puts heads 2 and 3 together at dimensions 42–51 and the readout at 52–61, so the constants line should read P3 = 42; it reads 52, the readout's first dimension. It stopped by its own choice after 22 tool calls and 6.4 minutes, well within the 60-minute, $2 per-run budget (no turn cap was set: Claude Code's --max-turns was not used). Its 2 replicates were identical in everything checked — the same files given to the agent (identical SHA-256 hashes), prompt, model (claude-haiku-5-5), Claude Code 2.1.330, effort and grading — so nothing the agent could see differed except the unseedable sampling (outside its view, the runs ran at different times and the server-side model behind the name cannot be verified); they reached accuracy 0.9994 and 0.9986. So the bug occurred in 1 of 3 identical runs: a chance slip that the setup does not force, whose frequency so few runs barely constrain (95 % Clopper–Pearson interval 1%–91%). The agent never found the bug: it blamed the neurons (“Bias-free ReLU neurons don't span cos(w(a+b)) well.”), tuned constants around the bug (self-test peak 0.7846) and then kept the setting it judged more faithful to the explanation (“I'll keep the faithful setting (penalty 10, slope 0.707, κ=0), which gives 0.56, and report the trade-off.”).
2.why_short: Right frequencies, wrong answers: a layout bug in Haiku's own script: head 3 wrote into the answer dimensions (P3 = RO = 52); fixing it gives accuracy 1.0000. The agent blamed the neurons and never found it (bug in 1 of 3 identical runs)
